title: An unusual presentation of carcinomatous meningitis
case_prompt: A 67-year-old man with no significant comorbidities presented with one week of progressive confusion on a background of three weeks of tension-type headaches. Three days before admission, a contrast-enhanced CT of the brain was normal. His history was notable only for stage IB superficial spreading melanoma and in-situ melanoma excised from the back and shoulder five years earlier, with no evidence of recurrence. On examination he was disoriented to time and place; vital signs were normal, and there were no meningeal signs, focal neurologic deficits, or new skin lesions. Laboratory studies showed a leukocyte count of 13.9×10^9/L with neutrophilia (12.1×10^9/L), C-reactive protein 8.5 mg/L, and otherwise normal chemistry, thyroid, and liver function tests. On Day 1, lumbar puncture revealed clear, straw-colored cerebrospinal fluid with a markedly low glucose of 0.4 mmol/L (reference 2.2–3.9), elevated protein of 4.0 g/L (reference <0.45), and a monocytic pleocytosis (20 leukocytes/mm^3, 19 monocytes, 1 neutrophil); Gram stain was negative. Non-contrast brain MRI showed possible communicating hydrocephalus. Empiric treatment for meningoencephalitis with intravenous benzylpenicillin, ceftriaxone, and acyclovir was initiated. All microbiology tests returned negative by Day 3, but as the patient’s condition worsened, empiric antituberculous therapy was started on Day 5. A repeat lumbar puncture demonstrated an opening pressure >30 cm H2O, bloodstained fluid, glucose 0.3 mmol/L, protein 2.3 g/L, leukocyte count 130/mm^3 (122 monocytes, 8 neutrophils) and 60 unidentified cells. Gadolinium-enhanced MRI of the brain revealed leptomeningeal enhancement within the interpeduncular cistern and communicating hydrocephalus.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Infectious meningoencephalitis was initially considered — “Following the LP, the patient was commenced on empirical treatment for meningoencephalitis with intravenous benzylpenicillin, ceftriaxone and acyclovir.”  
2. Bacterial and viral causes were excluded by negative studies — “results of all microbiology tests returned negative.”  
3. Tuberculous meningitis was considered due to marked hypoglycorrhachia and clinical deterioration — “empiric treatment for TB meningitis was commenced on Day 5.”  
4. Progressive hydrocephalus was included in the differential at this stage — “Differential diagnoses at this stage included progressive hydrocephalus and leptomeningeal disease.”  
5. Leptomeningeal disease was suspected based on contrast-enhanced MRI — “Gd-MRI showed probable leptomeningeal enhancement within the interpeduncular cistern of the midbrain.”  
6. Froin’s syndrome was considered because of elevated CSF protein and xanthochromia — “A CSF protein of 4 g/L is noteworthy as it raises the possibility of Froin’s syndrome... The presence of extensive spinal leptomeningeal disease further supports this hypothesis.”  
7. Carcinomatous meningitis was difficult to distinguish from TB meningitis because of overlapping CSF features — “The marked similarity in CSF analysis between TB meningitis and CM in the absence of malignant cytology can be diagnostically challenging.”
